items.why: Clearly separates the five takers from the priest and armed men waiting at the gate.
Tests the sequence of two takings, with the five men clearly acting before the priest.
Resolving “our” gives the trees, though “Whose ruler” makes an otherwise clear task awkward.
The excerpt explicitly links prosperity to plentiful resources, not merely similarity to the Sidonians.
Connects their search for a home to their lack of an allotted territory.
The stated fear gives a complete answer, but the task mostly repeats the opening sentence.
Requires distinguishing the relatives receiving instructions from the citizens meant to hear the message.
Distinguishes the stated search for lodging from the house he happens to reach.
Calls a conditional wish a “request” and mainly tests its position before another statement.
“Does something” and “the report” obscure the concrete action, leaving a contrived pronoun-identification task.
The report is identifiable, but going into the fields also involves coming out of the city.
The mother's quoted intention identifies her son, while the narrator later names the actual craftsman.
Readers can connect the unnamed man killed by his servant with Abimelek, named immediately afterward.
The deaths follow the deliberate burning with people inside, making the cause clear.
Distinguishes the priests' endpoint from the separate statement about how long the idol remained in use.
The shouting immediately accompanies the turn, supporting a clear explanation of the Danites' reaction.
Requires interpreting a rhetorical question as reluctance to give up valuable fruit.
Burning is the specific aim, but “attacking the tower” is also a true broader purpose.
The land is identifiable, but the question assumes a journey that the excerpt only urges the listeners to make.
Asks for Micah's stated reason for confidence, not the Levite's unrelated place of origin.
Ephraim contains the house rather than being a distinct previous stop, and the residence wording is needlessly convoluted.
The references to Jerub-Baal and “my father” identify the intended person without requiring outside knowledge.
The sender is explicit, so the question is clear but offers little beyond name retrieval.
Separates the priest being asked from God, whom the priest is asked to consult.
The curse describes the punishment, not a separate event that happens afterward.
“They” and “first claim” force readers to reconstruct the question before answering “shadows.”
The purpose is explicit, but “For what result” is awkward wording for ordinary readers.
Requires seeing that ruling would mean giving up the oil the tree values.
Readers must identify Micah's mother as the “you” in his report of the curse.
Clearly distinguishes eating and drinking at the festival from the earlier grape work.
Calls for two stated reasons help is unavailable: distance from Sidon and lack of outside ties.
